The spun-off unit is the parent's core earnings engine (≈51.0bn of ≈55.6bn separate revenue; all Legend of Mir trademarks/copyrights) and is entangled in pending litigation/arbitration in Korea, China and Singapore with Actoz, Shanda, Kaiying and Huanyou — ceding control is strategically unlikely and an IPO or sale is impractical while disputes are unresolved.

Counter-signals keep disposal probability well above zero: the Chinese pinyin name 'ChuanQi IP', a stock-option clause in the new company's articles that presupposes a future 기업공개, broad third-party allotment authority (up to 50% to foreign/strategic investors) and a full menu of redeemable/convertible preferred shares — a structure that could accommodate a Chinese strategic partner or an overseas listing once litigation settles.

Ring-fencing the IP licensing business into a dedicated vehicle is a common precursor to JV/settlement structures with Chinese licensees, but any such step within 3–5 years would most plausibly be a minority stake rather than loss of control; the single most likely outcome remains full retention.

reasons: The stated purpose explicitly includes selling newly issued shares of the spun-off company or attracting external investment, a direct management signal that 100% ownership is not intended to be permanent.
The filing itself warns that consolidated-statement effects may change depending on progress of the new-share sale / external investment, showing management already anticipates ownership dilution.

The carved-out EV business is tiny and early-stage (about 1.3bn KRW revenue vs 466bn KRW for the remaining camera-module business) and highly capital-intensive, while the parent carries ~181bn KRW liabilities including ~86bn short-term borrowings, so outside capital is the natural funding route.

The new company's articles pre-build investor instruments: dividend-preferred, convertible and redeemable class shares up to 50% of authorized shares, third-party allotments up to 30%, CB/BW up to 500bn KRW, and multiple clauses contingent on a future stock-market listing — a typical template prepared for VC/PE rounds and an eventual IPO.
The correction raising paid-in capital to 25bn KRW with 5,000 KRW par and 5m shares is consistent with tidying the cap table ahead of investor negotiations.

Counter-considerations: the subsidiary is established as unlisted with no re-listing, no buyer or investor is named, and a small EV startup faces real execution risk, so the parent could keep 100% if fundraising fails or the business is wound down.

The new company's articles of incorporation are pre-wired for venture financing: detailed RCPS/convertible/redeemable preferred share clauses (제8조의2~8조의5), third-party allotment up to 50% to 'financial institutions, partner companies, other investors', stock options up to 10%, CB/BW ceilings of 50bn KRW each, and even a clause for issuing shares for a KOSDAQ listing.

The parent is small and loss-making (accumulated deficit ≈ -44.5bn KRW, 8.4bn KRW current convertible bonds plus 5.5bn derivative liabilities, shares trading near 3,300–4,800 won) and cannot realistically self-fund a capital-intensive AI robotics venture; outside capital is the natural route.

The robotics unit is tiny and early-stage (capital 1bn KRW, net assets ~2.05bn, 8-month sales ~375m KRW) and is set up as a standalone startup with its own brand (UON Robotics), own website and a separate Daejeon headquarters — a structure suited to raising its own funding round.
